Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
schema.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
schema.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. **IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. # A Quarterback-Specific Model by Transfer Learning: Reported Failure

**What it is** — Burke's fourth variant tries to capture one passer's tendencies. The motive he gives: "we don't have enough data for individual quarterbacks, they just don't have enough pass attempts" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]). The method (EeBgUCYhezc [18:50]):

1. Train all layers on the full data set, all quarterbacks.
2. Freeze the base layers.
3. Retrain on one quarterback only.

He compares the shared layers to a common intuitive sense of physics (everyone can drive without crashing) and the retrained layers to individual executive decision-making (EeBgUCYhezc [19:21]). The result: "not as well as I'd hoped". Drew Brees (as named) was the most similar quarterback to Drew Brees, but some of the best-performing quarterbacks were the least similar and some of the poorest performers the most similar, on target-decision similarity (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]). He offers an explanation that Brees threw to running backs by design, while others do so "as a last resort" (EeBgUCYhezc [20:22]; the caption text here is garbled, so the explanation is uncertain). He reports it despite the result, calling this variant "pretty experimental" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]).

**Why it works** — It did not work as hoped, so there is no mechanism to give for success. The speaker gives the brain analogy above only as intent. Inference: the speaker says individual passers lack enough attempts, so retraining on one passer likely leaves too little to fit person-specific layers.

**When to apply** — As a cautionary case when someone proposes a per-athlete model from a small pooled data set (a single Baylor quarterback, one athlete's force-plate history). Ask first what the athlete-level sample size is and how similarity will be checked.

Eric's baseline: individual thresholds use "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q2a.) Inference: that is a simple within-person method, not a pooled-model fine-tune.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one reported attempt, in one data set (2016 to 2018 NFL passes), with no reported metric beyond the similarity ranking, so it should not be cited as proof that transfer learning cannot work for individualized models. It is also not a recommendation to use it. The speaker's explanation for the odd similarity ordering is unverified.

**Example** — The talk's own: the top five and bottom five "similar quarterbacks" ranking, in which Brees is most similar to himself (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]).

**Related** — [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]] (variant 4 is this); [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]].

# In Simulated Seasons Where ACWR Does Nothing, It Still Predicts Injury About as Strongly as the Literature Reports

**What it is** — The speakers report that in their real NFL and Italian-soccer data, ACWR (last 7 days of load over last 28 days) is "highly predictive of injury in a particular session" (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:12]). They then simulated 1,000 seasons per sport in which injury probability depended only on the intensity of the current session, so ACWR had no effect by construction (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43], [14:13]). In those simulations a chi-square test of ACWR against injury was "extremely highly significant" (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43]). The apparent increase in injury risk was 6.8% for the Italian team and 10.5% for the NFL team, which the speaker says is "about of the same order" as effects reported across sports in the literature (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]). The talk does not say whether 6.8% and 10.5% are relative or absolute, and the numbers come from auto-captions and were not checked against the slides. They also say the first published paper, on cricket bowlers, appeared in 2014 and has been cited over 250 times, and that hundreds of papers followed (TIRINmtZOu0 [06:36], [07:07], [07:38]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that a hard past week makes a hard session today likely, and today's intensity is what drives injury; see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The simulation itself is the evidence that the pattern can arise without any ACWR effect; the speakers do not show that it did arise that way in the published studies.

**When to apply** — When reading an ACWR injury paper or vendor claim: Inference: treat a reported ACWR effect of 5 to 10% as within what the schedule alone can produce in these two datasets. Inference: ask any vendor showing an ACWR risk curve whether it adjusts for the load of the session in which injury occurred. Eric's baseline: ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision, and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Two teams, two sports (NFL and a European club); no stated roster size, number of injuries or load variable, so do not read 6.8% and 10.5% as a college football estimate. The speakers say they have not disproved the field and that a more complex model might still find signal (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49], [23:35]). Their view that the products are "snake oil" is stated opinion near the start of the talk (TIRINmtZOu0 [01:01]). The simulation reproduces the association's size, not its shape: the talk does not show that the U-shape or the sweet spot (captions "08 and 1.3", probably 0.8 to 1.3, TIRINmtZOu0 [05:36]) arises from the artifact.

**Example** — The speakers' own: NFL 10.5% and Italian soccer 6.8% apparent increase in risk from a null simulation (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]).

**Related** — [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. Existing library, agrees in direction: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]] (acute load alone and random-denominator ratios performed like ACWR in Serie A data). ============================== claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed.md

# The post-concussion "window of vulnerability" is longer than return-to-play practice assumed

**What it is** — The speaker defines the window of vulnerability as the period after a concussion in which further physical or cognitive trauma is "much more damaging", slower to recover from and may lead to permanent deficits; his comparison is to playing on a broken leg (npgdKKdJSww [04:04], [04:34]). He says the window is "dramatically" longer than believed:
- In 2008 athletes were still being sent back within 15 minutes if symptoms cleared on the sideline (npgdKKdJSww [12:43]).
- The window in rats is 7 to 10 days (npgdKKdJSww [12:43], [13:13]).
- Research tests (magnetic resonance spectroscopy, fMRI, blood flow, evoked potentials) find that "no one seems to recover to baseline" on the hardest tests within 30 days, so "their brain is abnormal" (npgdKKdJSww [13:13], [13:43]).
- The working rule he describes is that an athlete abnormal against his baseline neuropsychological test cannot go back in (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]).

He cites a recent case (a pro hockey star still out; a basketball star back in three days) as a failure to respect the window (npgdKKdJSww [04:34], [05:04]). He flags his own claim as broad: with little time, he says, he is using broad concepts and asks the audience not to criticize the science (npgdKKdJSww [13:13]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that a concussion "starts a Cascade of events" that leaves the brain vulnerable (npgdKKdJSww [04:34]); he does not describe the cascade. Inference: the rat figure and the abnormal research scans are indirect evidence for a human clinical window, and the speaker moves from them to a longer clinical window without showing the link.

**When to apply** — As a reason to be wary of any return-to-play criterion built on clinical symptom clearance alone, and when a stakeholder asks why concussion return takes longer than other injuries. It is context for Athletic Medicine's process, not a rule for Applied Performance testing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance does not assess readiness in return to play: "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q22). The baseline holds no concussion criteria and no recovery-window rules.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use "no one recovers within 30 days" as a clinical return criterion: abnormal research imaging is not the same as unreadiness, and the speaker admits to broad strokes and to the 60-day figure being a hypothetical (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]). The rat window is animal data, with no human study shown. The speaker's "15 minutes in 2008" is a statement of past practice, not a cited study. The talk is from 2012; consensus guidance has changed, so check current guidelines with Athletic Medicine. Return-to-play decisions on concussion are medical decisions.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a basketball star "back in three days" after a concussion, described as "ridiculous" (npgdKKdJSww [05:04]); the speaker's view, not a measured case.

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the availability cost of taking this window seriously); [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries: what return-to-play criteria should include for non-concussion injuries; compare, do not merge).

============================== claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates.md

# Diagnosed concussion rates sit far below what surveys and sideline observers find

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Chris nowinsky", who also gives his background as a former Harvard football player and pro wrestler, npgdKKdJSww [01:00]) says that programs with athletic trainers diagnose about 5% of athletes per year in contact and collision sports, "one out of 20", while anonymous end-of-season surveys that leave out the word "concussion" and ask about symptoms after blows give numbers "more like 50%" (npgdKKdJSww [06:04]). He cites three further results, all second-hand and with garbled study names:
- A study (caption "langbert") in which the average person suffered "three dings per season" (npgdKKdJSww [06:34]).
- A hockey study (caption "eckan") of 16 to 21 year olds in which a doctor placed in the stands liberally pulled players who looked off and tested them with the standard tools: the speaker reports he found 35% ("one-third were pulled out") versus 5% in the usual trainer-only group, "seven times as many" concussions (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).
- An observer study in which stand observers saw about half the symptoms players reported; the captions give 33 versus 54 for a women's sample, with the unit unstated, so the figures are unclear (npgdKKdJSww [07:04]).

From these he estimates "we are probably diagnosing between two and 10% of concussions" (npgdKKdJSww [07:34]). The estimate is his own, not a measured rate.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the injury cannot be seen: concussion does not show on standard CT or MRI and diagnosis rests on signs and symptoms, so sports "get by" without removing athletes the way they would for a visible injury (npgdKKdJSww [05:04], [07:34]). Inference: a diagnosis count measures reporting and detection effort as much as incidence, which is why putting a doctor in the stands moved the count sevenfold.

**When to apply** — When someone quotes a diagnosed-concussion rate as the incidence of the injury, or when judging whether an Athletic Medicine count captures most events. Inference: an anonymous symptom survey at season end, asked without the word "concussion", is the comparison the speaker's own data points to.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletic Medicine's decisions with information rather than making them (Explicit, Playbook p.6; interview 2026-09-28, Q4: "Testing and progression. I collaborate on loading and progression decisions when needed. It doesn't really end."), and no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). The baseline holds no concussion criteria, so this entry is a comparison point, not a method Eric uses.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not read 50% as the rate of medically diagnosable concussion; surveys count self-reported symptoms after blows. The hockey sample is 16 to 21 year olds, and the speaker gives no sample sizes for any of the three studies. The speaker discloses a consultant role and a financial tie to the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]). The talk is from 2012, so detection practice and rules have changed since. Do not carry the rates to Baylor football without Athletic Medicine's own counts. Anything diagnostic belongs to Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance does not set concussion criteria.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the hockey study, where adding one observer with pull-out authority took the identified share from 5% to 35% (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the speaker's own consequence of closing this gap); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]]; [[funk-2025-an-analysis-of-guardian-cap-use-and-changes-in-the-concussion-rate-in-national-football-le]] (NFL preseason practice concussion rates, an exposure-based cohort).

# Familiarity carries over between seasons with diminishing marginal gains

**What it is** — Asked about diminishing returns, a speaker answers that a third season would start lower than the peak at the end of season two but "not that different from the start of the second season", so marginal gains keep declining season to season (o4rMbhsdk0I [19:31]). The data set does not hold enough pairs who played together for long to find a theoretical maximum, but "two, three seasons together is beneficial" (o4rMbhsdk0I [20:01]). The speakers state that the presented curve restarts above zero in year two (about 5% above the first-season start, o4rMbhsdk0I [10:14]) and that the starting points and the number of shots needed to get past the steep part differ by season, while the general shape stays the same (o4rMbhsdk0I [37:59], [38:30]).

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism. Inference: the pattern fits a pair that keeps some of what it learned over the offseason and forgets some.

**When to apply** — As a rough expectation when weighing roster continuity: keeping a pair or unit together carries some gain forward, with the largest gain in the first stretch. Inference: for football, this supports tracking which units return intact before judging early-season output.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speakers' answer to an audience question about a slide, backed by a described extrapolation, not by a shown third-season analysis (o4rMbhsdk0I [19:31]), so confidence is untested. The speakers say the model has no notion of breaks within a season and that decay after injury is untested (o4rMbhsdk0I [33:19], [33:49]). Inference: do not use this to predict a returning starter's rust or a return-to-performance timeline. Asked whether to trade for pairs of players, a speaker said no (it raises risk) and that trading money for talent is a much bigger effect (o4rMbhsdk0I [39:02], [39:32]), so it is not a basis for trade value either.

**Example** — The speakers' description: third-season start sits near the second-season start, below the end of season two (o4rMbhsdk0I [19:31]).

# Four Ways to Measure Hormones, Four Sets of Limits

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari," an endocrinologist) summarizes the limits of each sampling route, prompted by patients bringing printouts from a $1,000 blood test and a claim that a wearable "has been validated against these hormones" (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:17] to [31:47]). Her questions for any such test: what assay was used, how was it tested, and how was the sample stored (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47]).
- **Saliva:** cheap, but needs many measures on multiple days (frequent sampling), and validation is weaker because "those assays aren't that great yet" (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47]).
- **Blood:** more expensive and involves a needle, so not done daily, but gives precise hormone quantification. Timing matters: the cycle phase at the draw, and hormones that differ morning versus afternoon (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47] to [32:17]).
- **Dried blood spot:** you cannot check a thousand hormones from a spot "right now"; it needs repeated sampling and performs well with some moderate concentrations of certain hormones, with caution (an7u-tVP5Xc [32:17] to [32:48]).
- **Urine:** easy to collect and extensively validated against serum, but expensive to analyze every day; good as a profiling tool for patterns over a month or two, not exact concentrations (an7u-tVP5Xc [32:48]).

# Long Shots Cause Long Rebounds, but Not More Fast Breaks: Rim-Area Misses Lead to Fast Breaks 1.5 to 2 Times as Often

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests the claim that "long shots lead to long rebounds and allow fast breaks" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:35]). Part true: a longer shot comes off the rim harder, so the rebound is longer (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:35]). Part not: using 15 to 20 years of data, a shot from around the rim that is rebounded "is between one and a half and two times more likely to lead to a fast break than an above the break three"; a corner three is "slightly more fast breakable" but much less so than a missed shot in the paint (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:07]). His account of why we remember it wrongly: the vivid case (a defender closes out, the shooter misses, the defender sprints for a layup) sticks in memory (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39]). His explanation of the real pattern: a three usually follows "good execution, good spacing", the floor is balanced, "there's always someone back on defense", and an above-the-break shooter is "already halfway back" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39], [08:10]).

**Why it works** — The data finding (the 1.5 to 2 times comparison) is the speaker's reported result. The explanation about balanced spacing is his own hypothesis: he introduces it with "what I think is happening" and the talk does not test it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39], [08:10]).

**When to apply** — As an example of separating an observed rate from a mechanism story. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: a coach's in-game belief ("that always happens") can be checked against stored game data before changing a plan, if the data are available.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported for the rate comparison, untested for the mechanism. The speaker gives no sample sizes, intervals or season-level breakdown, and the figures are described from slides. NBA data only. The "one and a half to two times" range is spoken as one comparison across 15 to 20 years; he does not say whether the ratio changed over the period. Do not generalize to college or to other sports, and do not present the balanced-floor story as established.

**Example** — From the talk: a missed above-the-break three, with the shooter already halfway back, against a missed rim-area shot where the defense is often out of position (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:07], [08:10]).

# Rest alone for partial UCL tears: 93% of 43 players returned without surgery, and tear location may predict who fails

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes two team-physician studies of the league's own players, in the area of conservative care and rehab where he sees "very promising studies" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:42], [18:13]):
- The Colorado Rockies' study of players with partial UCL tears, in the middle ground between a full tear that means surgery and an injury that might not need it: after six to eight weeks of rest, 93% came back and pitched without surgery (caption: "pitched with that name surgery", read as without surgery). The sample was 43 players, and the speaker says "it's tough to really draw too many conclusions from that" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:13], [18:43]). 93% of 43 is about 40 players (Inference, my arithmetic).
- A similar study by a Cleveland Indians physician (name garbled in the captions) asked whether the location of the tear predicts who returns: players with distal tears were "much more likely to fail the rehab" and need surgery than players with proximal tears (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:43], [19:14]).

His takeaway: the medical community is getting "more strategic and accurate" about which injuries lend themselves to conservative care and which "you probably should just opt for the surgery and kind of come back more quickly" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [19:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a partial tear can heal or fail, and tear location sorts the two groups; the studies as reported do not show how, and the rest window is the same 6 to 8 weeks that the orthobiologic users also wait (see the evidence-lag entry).

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask Athletic Medicine whether a defined rest window before testing is reasonable for a partial injury, and what Applied Performance testing would show at the end of it. This is a question for Athletic Medicine, not a recommendation.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletic Medicine's decisions with information and contributes "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6; interview 2026-09-28, Q4). The baseline does not state criteria for return, and the written protocol (UE and LE rehab templates) has not been read by Flint.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: one team's 43 players, no control group, no stated follow-up period or definition of "came back", and one team-physician study each, none peer-review-checked in the talk. Baseball elbow only; a UCL tear is not a football soft-tissue or joint injury. Do not treat 93% as the chance of a partial tear healing. Clinical decisions belong to Athletic Medicine. ============================== claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football.md

# Cutting contact in practice is the main lever on head-impact exposure

**What it is** — The speaker's stated focus is "reducing hitting in practice", the "number one way" to restrict total counts, because in football "up to 75%" of brain trauma exposure happens in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). He gives three policy moves as evidence that people are "buying in":
- In the NFL collective bargaining talks the players' union pushed for 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]).
- The Ivy League followed: NCAA rules allow five days of hitting a week and the Ivy League chose two, with an intent to push lower (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).
- Pop Warner's executive director announced a plan to cut hitting from six hours a week to two by the next season (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

He says he sat on both the NFL-side and Ivy League committees and "pushed these like crazy" (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]), and that some limit on how many contact sports a child plays in a year is likely to follow (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is arithmetic on exposure: practices outnumber games, so most hits occur there (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The 75% figure comes with no source or method in the talk. Inference: contact in practice is also the exposure a program controls directly, which is why it is a lever where game contact is not.

**When to apply** — When a contact-practice schedule is being set or reviewed and the discussion is about how many contact periods, not about equipment. Inference: Applied Performance could log contact periods per practice by position group (practice minutes with contact, not impacts) and report them weekly to Athletic Medicine and coaches, as a record, not a cap.

Eric's baseline: progressions in volume and intensity are kept smooth and abrupt changes are treated as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); Applied Performance supports Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions with information (Explicit, Playbook p.6). The in-season week is set by the staff: lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q15). The baseline holds no contact-practice rule and no concussion criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — The 75% is an assertion, and it is "up to" for football only (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The three policy examples are the speaker's account of NFL, Ivy League and youth practice, with the speaker involved in two of them; none reports an outcome. College or Baylor practice schedules are not described, and contact definitions would have to be agreed with coaches. The talk gives no evidence that limiting contact reduces concussions; it gives the exposure logic and the policy trend. **Example** — The speaker's own: Pop Warner moving from six hours of weekly contact to two (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

============================== claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting.md

# Scheme Is a Confounder the Model Only Partly Handles

**What it is** — In Q&A a questioner points out that a blitzing linebacker has a much higher probability of being in a high-EPA play than a linebacker who is dropping into coverage, so scheme could confound the metric, and the data did not include play calls (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:13]). Ben Jenkins replies that knowing the scheme and each player's responsibility on the play is ongoing research, and that one way the model partly captures it is propensity weighting: if a defender has a very low chance of being involved and makes a tackle, that play gets higher weight, which reduces some of the bias. With scheme data he says the estimates would improve quite a bit (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13], [12:43]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's claim is that the propensity score absorbs how likely a defender is to be involved, which scheme partly determines (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). He does not show that the propensity model recovers assignments. Inference: the weighting can only correct for scheme to the extent the tracking features (positions, speeds, directions) reveal it before the tackle, so an assignment that looks the same as another cannot be separated.

**When to apply** — As the first question to ask of any defender-level number: which players' roles make the event more likely? Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): the coach's eye "can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further" (Explicit). **Example** — The questioner's: a blitzing linebacker versus a dropping one (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43]). The speaker's partial answer: low-probability tackler gets more weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]).

============================== claim--sleep-hours-predicted-injury-in-high-school-athletes.md

# Hours of Sleep Was the Strongest Predictor of Injury in a High School Athlete Study

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says high school athletes were followed for about 22 months and the number of hours of sleep gave the strongest prediction of the likelihood of injury; sleeping less than 8 hours raised injury likelihood by "1.7%" in the captions, a figure that may be garbled (for instance a ratio versus a percent) and should not be relied on (J7smyg1Czik [04:38], [05:08]). She names no authors, journal or sample size. She adds that reaction time rises and visual acuity falls with too little sleep, which she says makes injury more likely, and that the hormones needed for recovery are mostly secreted in sleep (J7smyg1Czik [05:08], [05:40]).

**Why it works** — Her stated reasoning is slower reaction time and poorer visual acuity, plus reduced recovery hormones (J7smyg1Czik [05:08]). These are asserted as plausible links; the talk does not show them as mediators in the injury study. Inference: an association in adolescents can reflect other things that travel with short sleep (training volume, school load).

**When to apply** — As a reason to record sleep when injury data are collected, not as a prediction rule. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model exists, and nothing objective is tracked for recovery or sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q12 and Q23, Explicit). Inference: this claim, if confirmed against its source, is a candidate variable to log first; the source must be identified before it is cited.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: one unnamed study, high school athletes, the key number is unreadable in the captions, and the study design, injury definition and adjustment are not described. High school findings do not transfer to NCAA football without checking. Do not quote "1.7%". Related work in the library on college athletes' sleep and nap behavior should be consulted before using any sleep and injury statement.

**Example** — The speaker's own description: high school athletes followed for about 22 months, with hours of sleep as the strongest predictor of injury (J7smyg1Czik [04:38], [05:08]).

# Make a Team-Level Match Model Sensitive to the Starting Eleven

**What it is** — The reward in the team-selection framework is expected points for a match. The presenters (Ryan Beiel and, in recorded video, the lead author Greg Everett, caption spellings) compute it from an adapted Maher model (caption "Maya"), a common soccer prediction model that assumes each team's scoring rate follows a Poisson distribution and learns offensive and defensive strengths from historical data to get win, draw and loss probabilities (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:05]). The original model works at team level and ignores individual selections, so they replaced the team-identity features with player-based numerical features: a player contribution model (caption "VAPE", likely a value-of-actions style model, not confirmed) supplies each player's skill value, and the combined skills of the chosen eleven feed a linear model (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]). ============================== framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models.md

# CLIP: A Doubly Robust Estimate of What Allowing Pressure Does to Completion

**What it is** — CLIP (caption versions: "causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays" and "...lineman..."; pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30]) estimates how pressure allowed by an offensive lineman changes completion probability, per lineman, per play, every tenth of a second (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30], [04:31]). Two models (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01], [10:35]):

1. **Outcome model:** probability of a completed pass from features X and whether pressure was allowed.
2. **Propensity score model:** probability that the lineman allows pressure, from features X. Inverse propensity weighting uses it to build a more balanced data set for comparing outcomes (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [10:35]).

The estimator is called doubly robust because "it only requires one of the two models to be correctly specified" to identify the causal effect (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01]). The captions name it "a w robust estimator" (garbled; the name is not confirmed here). The target is the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) per player per play: expected completion given pressure occurred minus expected completion given it did not, given features X (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31]). Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a 0 to 1 probability, which is what lets his plots show shading (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [13:35]). Inputs are Big Data Bowl tracking data for all linemen, teammates and opponents, with the model "figure out what was important"; he accounts for proximity to the quarterback, to the nearest defenders and to nearby teammates, and for defenders' position, speed and distance to the quarterback (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [11:05], [11:35]). A questioner said the features were confusing (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [11:05]). Summarizing for a questioner: it analyzes the propensity to allow pressure combined with the impact on completion given pressure, "in simple terms" yes (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [10:05]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's two stated advantages: it is "robust to model misspecification" and it "helps reduce bias from confounding variables" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31]). The talk gives no further mechanism for how the player-level credit is derived from the two models.

**When to apply** — As the reference when asking how a causal player metric is built from observational tracking data: name the treatment (pressure allowed), the outcome (completion), the two models, and the estimand (CATE). Its checks are in [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]].

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: the staff question that would justify this build is who on the offensive line is costing the offense, and the talk does not compare its cost with simpler views.

**When NOT to apply** — Needs play-level x,y tracking for all players at consistent quality, which the speaker says exists at the college level via computer vision (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:35]) but which the baseline's stack does not list. The public sample is the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season (caption "2020 2021") from the 2023 Big Data Bowl (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:03]); no play counts, player counts or intervals are given. The speaker's feature handling is loose by his own account. Causal claims hold only if the model adjusts for what drives both pressure and completion, and this is checked partly (see the robustness entry). He works at Sumer Sports, so this is the builder's view.

**Example** — The two worked plays in [[case-study--clip-failed-block-versus-clean-protection-plays]].

**Related** — [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]]; [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]. # Measuring familiarity: a shot-quality baseline plus two shared-attempt counters

**What it is** — The speakers' method for measuring how pairs get better together has two steps.
1. **Build an expected-points baseline.** A shot-probability model uses shot type, location, and NBA-supplied pressure scores at three levels (pressure on the passer, on the receiver, and on the shooter, defined by how close defenders are) (o4rMbhsdk0I [06:06], [06:37]). Expected points are the made-shot probability times 2 or 3 (o4rMbhsdk0I [07:08]). They tried XGBoost (best fit), random forest ("weird results") and logistic regression ("just wasn't quite as good") (o4rMbhsdk0I [06:37], [07:08]). Calibration by shot zone is shown on a slide.
2. **Regress on shared-attempt counters.** For every shot, regress expected points on two counters of how often that passer-shooter pair has gone passer to shooter on a catch-and-shoot attempt: one within the season and one cumulative across seasons, in a basic log-log form (o4rMbhsdk0I [08:40], [09:13]). The two counters let the model separate in-season change from season-to-season change.
3. **Split gain into selection and accuracy.** Repeat with actual points minus expected points as the outcome, assuming a 1.2 expected-points baseline (o4rMbhsdk0I [12:18]).

**Why it works** — Putting the baseline in expected points keeps shot choice (what quality of shot) apart from shot execution (whether it goes in). The speakers do not give a statistical argument for the log-log form beyond calling it simple and basic (o4rMbhsdk0I [08:40]).

**When to apply** — When asking whether a group of pairs improves with repetition: first fix a baseline that prices the opportunity, then count shared repetitions. Inference: in football this needs a play-level expected-value or grade baseline for the chosen play type and a reliable tally of shared reps for each pair. Eric's baseline: testing protocols must be exactly repeatable over time or the data cannot be trusted for comparison (course team position, speaker unconfirmed, Inferred); the same holds for how attempts are counted here.

**When NOT to apply** — The speakers call this a first step and say the model has no notion of breaks within a season (o4rMbhsdk0I [33:19], [33:49]), no controls for age, rookie status or role (o4rMbhsdk0I [35:23]), and no shot-frequency count outside catch-and-shoot combinations (o4rMbhsdk0I [34:19]). They report an interaction between season and attempt count that is statistically significant but changes the shape little (o4rMbhsdk0I [37:59]). The talk shows no controls for selection into shared playing time for pairs; it names that bias only for lineups, because good lineups play more together (o4rMbhsdk0I [31:16]). Treat the design as a template, and validate any new version on your own data.

**Example** — The talk's own use: 1600 pairs with 10 to 50 attempts, most frequent pair 237 attempts (caption spelling "Tyrese and Miles"), 2023-24 (o4rMbhsdk0I [07:38]).

# Audit the Female-Athlete Literature on Six Fields Before Trusting It

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari," a sports doctor and endocrinologist, an7u-tVP5Xc [13:21]) says her group and collaborators audit literature against set standards: pick a topic, find every paper with search terms, screen, then record (an7u-tVP5Xc [14:53] to [16:56]):
1. **Population:** men, women, biological females or males; how the population was defined and confirmed (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:23]).
2. **Athlete caliber:** tier 0 sedentary, tier 1 moving a little, tier 2 working out at least three times a week with the intention of competing at least once a year ("not a big step"), up to tier 5 world class. She also asks whether the paper reports physical activity level at all (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:23] to [15:54]). The captions garble the tier 0 and tier 1 wording; tiers 3 and 4 are not described.
3. **Menstrual status:** how it was determined (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:54] to [16:25]); see the principle entry on asking versus testing.
4. **Research theme:** performance or health (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]).
5. **Study impact:** the journal's impact factor (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25] to [16:56]).
6. **Sample size:** "nine women or 9,000 women" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:56]).

Purpose: understand how well female athletes are represented, find performance level and menstrual status handling, highlight strengths and problems without "dissing" earlier work, mine past work for questions, and track trends across subdisciplines and time (an7u-tVP5Xc [17:27] to [17:58]). The audit was run on 2011 to 2013 papers and again on 2021 to 2023 papers (an7u-tVP5Xc [17:58] to [18:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that studies often just say "women" or "men," so the fields force each paper to show who was studied and how (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:54]). The audit results she reports from this method are in the claim entry on audit results.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a screening grid when a coach or athlete cites a study about a women's team, to see at once whether the participants resemble collegiate athletes (her tier 2 and above), how menstrual status was determined, and how large the sample was. Inference: it can also be applied to the Zotero library for any women's-sport question. Eric's baseline: none; method-baseline.md states no rule for appraising outside studies.

**When NOT to apply** — The caliber tiers are described only partly in the transcript, so a tier-by-tier coding needs her published scheme (not in the talk). The audit topic coverage and number of papers are not stated. The fields describe reporting quality, not whether a result is true. Not designed for male or mixed-sex football studies, though the population and sample-size fields transfer.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the finding that 99.5% of supplement studies did not categorize or standardize menstrual cycle came from applying field 3 (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:56]). Inference: a paper that says only "women" without caliber or menstrual status would have gaps in fields 2 and 3.

============================== framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline.md

# Pass-Rush Pressure in Three Stages: Identify, Match, Score

**What it is** — S Min Hong (caption spelling "s Min Hong", "S Hong"; an applied scientist at AWS) presents work with the NFL Next Gen Stats team that replaces end-of-play pass-rush counts with a pressure measure through the whole play (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:00], [01:02]). Three problems are solved in sequence (1nt8hK2oYrE [02:38], [03:10], [03:42]):

1. **Blocker and rusher identification.** Label each player's role in the first seconds of the play.
2. **Rusher-blocker matchup.** Who blocks whom, including double teams ("Russia can be double teamed", caption for "rusher") and rushers left open.
3. **Pressure score.** An instantaneous 0 to 1 pressure probability across the play (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]).

Stages 1 and 2 automate what "human labelers" did by watching each clip, to save cost and manual labor (1nt8hK2oYrE [05:44], [06:15]). Inputs are static features (normalized initial positions at the snap, roles) and dynamic ones (position, velocity, acceleration, direction), standardized before training (1nt8hK2oYrE [06:46]). The data are the public Big Data Bowl tracking data (positions over time, velocity, acceleration, play outcomes) (1nt8hK2oYrE [04:12], [04:42], [05:14]).

Reported results: F1 of 0.99 for identification and "close 0.91" for matchup (caption spelling; 1nt8hK2oYrE [07:47]). Two model types were promising. The chosen one models the two tasks one after the other; the model name is garbled in captions ("Orum", "autog glom"), so the model type is unconfirmed (1nt8hK2oYrE [07:17], [07:47]). A graph neural network (players as nodes, relationships as edges) performed worse but was kept as a future direction because one model could do both tasks (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:17]). Ground truth for who blocks whom was hand labels from the NFL and PFF (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:08]), and the framework handles double and triple teams (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the staging: you cannot score pressure on a rusher until you know who is rushing and who is blocking him. Inference: splitting the problem lets stages 1 and 2 be validated against hand labels (F1) while stage 3 has no direct label.

**When to apply** — As a template for any play-level model that needs a role label before an outcome score: validate each stage separately against human labels where they exist and report the stage that has no label as such.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: the build is justified only if defensive-line or protection staff have a question that end-of-play counts cannot answer. Baseline has no football pass-rush or position-tracking method to compare.

**When NOT to apply** — NFL tracking data and PFF hand labels; the baseline's technology stack (Catapult, Perch, Polar, VALD) lists no play-level tracking and labeling pipeline for football games. The F1 values are caption-rough and from one data set; the speaker gives no sample sizes. The model "didn't account for" team scheme or rushing and blocking strategy (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). Stage 3 has no accuracy figure (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a Jets versus Cowboys clip in which end-of-play stats credit only the players who recorded sacks, while other players closed on the quarterback without credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:32], [02:05]).

**Related** — [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]. A different tracking-data method on the same side of the ball: [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]] scores offensive linemen causally (SSAC25), while this pipeline is a descriptive, per-rusher pressure model. Library paper on the same problem: [[pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance]].

============================== framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft.md

# A prospective cohort: baseline tests at entry, then follow every athlete through the medical record

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes the league's most significant research project with the players association: when a player is drafted he is asked for a baseline set (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:08]):
- A shoulder and elbow MRI.
- A full biomechanical evaluation.
- A playing-history questionnaire.

Each player is then followed for the rest of his career for performance, usage and future injuries, to see whether any baseline test or later behavior predicts injury, which can then inform preventive programs (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). The design depends on the league's electronic medical record: since 2010 all clubs must use it, so the league does not need to keep going back to players to ask whether they were injured, which he says eliminates any participation or dropout rate (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [16:39]). So far 225 players are enrolled, with about 400 expected when baseline collection finishes (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11]). The research partners are the players association, club medical staff and an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins; data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]).

The committee's research questions, listed separately from this study (the speaker does not tie them to it) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [10:25], [11:26], [11:57], [12:30]): at the professional level, whether biomechanics, usage or velocity matter as risk factors; whether the rehab process or future usage can reduce second surgeries; whether surgical variants (graft, technique) affect success; and whether alternative therapies can shorten the 12 to 16 month rehab or avoid surgery.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the record removes loss to follow-up, one of the main weaknesses of long cohort studies (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). Inference: baseline data recorded before any injury is what lets a later injury be compared to something measured earlier; the 2015 spring-training study could not do this because it met pitchers only after they had returned (AgouMNTeyo4 [29:22]).

**When to apply** — When deciding what to record at entry for each athlete so that later injuries can be studied: a short history of prior workload and injury, the physical baselines already collected, and a way to link them to later records.

Eric's baseline: each source system holds its own data and the source wins over the aggregating platform (Kitman) when they disagree (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q11); there is no common testing cadence across sports (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q9); no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, Q12). Data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: a Baylor version would be a small intake record linked to existing VALD and GPS data, not an MRI program, and its value depends on the consistency of collection that Eric's NordBord decision stressed.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the talk reports design and enrollment only, with no results. The data are not public, so the claims cannot be checked. It rests on a league-wide record system that every club must use (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]); Baylor's follow-up would depend on its own record system and on a stable staff. Teams also guard training data as a competitive advantage, so the league works with a select group of teams on granular training data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:44]). Professional draftees, not college athletes. The speaker works for the league office. Do not add collection until a question exists.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 225-player enrollment, with follow-up by the medical record rather than by contacting players (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39], [17:11]).

**Related** — [[case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured]] (2015 talk: a post-hoc comparison with no pre-injury data); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]].

============================== framework--weight-mixed-unit-components-by-correlation-with-an-outcome.md

# Weight Mixed-Unit Components by Their Correlation With an Accepted Outcome

**What it is** — The overall receiver score combines open, catch and YAC components with different units: YAC is in yards above expected, the others are residual catch-probability style quantities, so there is a "unit mismatch" (teg9SfzpMy0 [36:32]). The panel's solution:
- **Weights differ by position:** receivers and tight ends are slightly different, running backs very different (teg9SfzpMy0 [36:02], [36:32]).
- **Target outcome:** yards per route run, described as probably the best conventional statistic for grading a receiver's season (teg9SfzpMy0 [37:03]).
- **Rule:** each component's proportion in the overall score is set by how well it correlated with yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [37:03]).
- **Scale:** components are normalized (z-scores) and mapped to a 0 to 99 score for fan readability, like ESPN's QBR; extreme seasons are clipped (a 99 might actually be a 105) (teg9SfzpMy0 [42:14], [42:44], [43:15]).

**Why it works** — The panel's reasoning is practical: a conventional outcome statistic provides a way to decide how much each skill matters (teg9SfzpMy0 [37:03]). The captions give no weights. Inference: weighting by correlation with an outcome makes the composite resemble that outcome, so the composite adds little if the outcome is the thing being judged.

**When to apply** — When building a composite from components in different units. Inference: pick an accepted outcome first, standardize the components, and weight by relation to the outcome, stating the outcome. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): coach-facing reports are built by strength staff for most teams (Explicit). Inference: a composite handed to those staff needs its weighting rule written down in plain terms.

**When NOT to apply** — No weights, correlations or sample sizes are given (teg9SfzpMy0 [37:03]). `untested`. A panelist says that for a team they would use a more sophisticated final number or set of units than the fan scale (teg9SfzpMy0 [42:44]). Clipping hides large differences, which the panel shows with Deebo Samuel's 2021 YAC season (caption "Debo Samuel"), where the next best season would be about 60 against his 99 (teg9SfzpMy0 [43:15]). Requires an outcome statistic that is trusted, which Eric would need to name for his own use.

**Example** — The panel's: the YAC scale clipped because one season (Samuel, 2021) was so large (teg9SfzpMy0 [43:15]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--name-a-metric-for-what-it-measures-and-scale-it-for-the-audience]], [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]].

============================== heuristic--fatigue-is-individual-read-it-next-day-with-trainer-knowledge.md

# Fatigue is individual: read it with people who know the athlete, and read it the next day

**What it is** — Asked how coaches and parents know when a pitcher has reached the fatigue level, Glenn Fleisig answers in his Q&A (AgouMNTeyo4 [49:59], [50:29]):
- His group tried to measure fatigue scientifically from muscle activity, "it doesn't work".
- Pitcher and coach cannot figure it out at the moment of the game; they need to know each other beforehand (a tough guy, recent problems, how he walks after getting hurt), and no one wants a player pitching while thinking "I think it hurts a little" (AgouMNTeyo4 [50:29]).
- What is decided is not at game time but afterward: in the training room the trainers are "a key for reading when a guy is better, when it is normal and when it's not normal". A pitcher who used to need two days of recovery and now needs three is a signal; he says pro teams will skip or bump a start on trainer feedback (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).
- The athlete's education is for the next day: pain in the elbow or shoulder is not normal; full-body fatigue is normal; feeling full-body fatigue in the game "is your body saying let's call it a day" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30], [52:01]).
- Summary line: "fatigue is individual" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no data for this answer; it is his stated practice among the pro teams and trainers he talks to. Inference: it uses the one signal he trusts, a person who sees the athlete every day and compares to that athlete's own normal, which fits a result that fatigue behavior was the largest risk marker while no instrument measured it.

**When to apply** — When a monitoring system needs an escalation path: define who reads the athlete the next day, what counts as a change from his own normal (recovery taking longer, pain versus tiredness), and what action follows a flag.

Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit); a trained eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and mRSI from daily CMJ testing replaced them as the readiness marker (Explicit, same source). Inference: Fleisig's answer partly conflicts with the mRSI choice, since it relies on trainer and athlete report; Eric's practice keeps subjective input only where context is needed, such as return to play. Recovery is managed through load design, with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23).

**When NOT to apply** — Assertion from one expert answer, not tested; he says himself that measurement attempts failed. It presumes trainers or coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens after a flag. Pitching context: one start every fifth day, with a next-day check; do not copy the "next day" timing to football's weekly cycle without Baylor's own staff routine. Self-report can be gamed (Eric's survey experience above). Fatigue and pain are not distinguished by any test in the talk.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a pitcher whose recovery moved from two days to three, which the trainer notices and which can lead the team to skip a start (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).

**Related** — [[claim--pitching-while-fatigued-is-the-largest-retrospective-odds]]; [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] (Old Bull).

# Check a Player-Value Model With Expected-Direction Tests When No Ground Truth Exists

**What it is** — Paul Sabin offers three plots "to validate some of our assumptions and some of our results" (oZsFyPGij0U [17:30], [18:03]).
1. **Separation check.** Quarterback value against average offensive-line value: correlated, "not as strong as you would think," with teams that have strong lines and weak quarterbacks and the reverse (oZsFyPGij0U [18:03], [18:34]).
2. **Within-unit check.** The two linemen with the most snaps: correlated but "not perfectly," so credit can be split between them (oZsFyPGij0U [18:34]).
3. **Direction-of-change check.** Value at the new team against the old team for players who moved. College transfers fall above the one-to-one line (better at the new school); NFL movers fall below it (typically a bit worse, which he links to players nearing 30 whose teams let them go) (oZsFyPGij0U [19:05], [19:35]).
The slopes and correlations are shown only as plots; no numbers are given in the transcript. He also treats a backup center doing worse than the starter as support for the center result (oZsFyPGij0U [21:39], [22:09]).

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") says "you've got to start with surveys," but to be careful how they are built (an7u-tVP5Xc [27:41]).
- **Strengths:** cheap, early dissemination, large cohorts, assess prevalence, and results can show correlations that inspire later investigation (an7u-tVP5Xc [27:41] to [28:12]).
- **Weaknesses:** cross-sectional so no causal conclusion; selection bias; recall bias; non-response bias (an7u-tVP5Xc [28:12]).

# Baseball Analogies Break Where a Basketball Possession Can End With No Shot at All

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says many concepts port from baseball to basketball: rate stats over counting stats, efficiency, and treating the possession or shot like a plate appearance (BJkCqf6Fj2w [12:48], [13:18]). Past a certain level of detail, two differences matter (BJkCqf6Fj2w [13:18], [13:48], [14:18]):
- **No batting order.** In baseball "one through nine hits", but in basketball "there aren't turns"; a hot player can shoot every time down the court.
- **A third outcome.** A baseball plate appearance ends safe or out; a shot is made or missed, but "a very important third possibility" is "not shoot at all". "There's no equivalent of a pass in baseball."
Consequence he draws: "a lot of what we would see as having a shot been contested well means that a player doesn't shoot at all" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18]). He cites the corner three as the example: it is one of the most valuable shots yet a small share of attempts, "because you have to do something right beforehand" and the defense is trying to stop it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:48]).

============================== principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation.md

# Prediction Is Not Attribution in Defensive Evaluation

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, as he introduces himself) argues that football has a "defensive attribution problem" (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). On a running play tackled for a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler, though several defenders contributed (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00], [00:31]). He contrasts two model types. A supervised model asks what will happen, is correlation-based, minimizes prediction error, and in his words "often confuses correlation with causation," is biased toward high-volume tacklers, and struggles to separate skill from opportunity (JHgeEo3n1do [01:01], [01:31]). A causal model asks what would happen if the defender had not made the tackle, which he says isolates individual contributions, accounts for situational context, and separates player effect from team and scheme effects (JHgeEo3n1do [01:31], [02:01]). His bottom line is that prediction is different from attribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the contrast: a predictive model optimizes error loss, not an estimate of one player's contribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). He gives no further mechanism for why high-volume tacklers are favored. Inference: a defender who is often near the ball will correlate with good outcomes whether or not he caused them, and a loss function that only rewards prediction accuracy has no reason to separate the two.

**When to apply** — When a number is going to be read as "this player caused this result" (contract, grade, or scheme decisions, which the speaker lists as uses at JHgeEo3n1do [10:11]) and the underlying model was fit only to predict an outcome. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12) says ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit).
